saving-unit: % of compressor output lost to leaks (before -> after)
note: Leaks sometimes waste 20-30% of output; a poorly maintained plant typically 20% of capacity; proactive leak detection and repair reduces leaks to less than 5-10% of output. Leakage >10% indicates improvement potential (p.29). Compressor controls must be re-evaluated to realize savings.

measure: Reduce compressor discharge pressure (per 2 psi, 100 psig systems)
note: About 1% per 2 psi at full output flow, plus 0.6-1.0% from reduced unregulated use (leaks, open blowing) where unregulated usage is 30-50% of demand. Differs for centrifugal and two-stage lubricant-injected screw compressors.

measure: Pressure/flow controller downstream of the primary receiver
saving-unit: % energy reduction (printed as 10 percent or more)
note: Where most end uses had not been properly pressure regulated; presumes compressor controls handle the reduced demand.

measure: Most efficient (premium) motor on a compressor
note: Because of heavy duty and load cycles it almost always makes sense to buy the most efficient motor available.

saving-unit: % of available heat recovered (80-93% of electricity becomes heat)
note: About 50,000 Btu/h available per 100 cfm of capacity at full load. Example (p.59): 100-hp compressor, 2 shifts 5 days (4,160 h/yr), 80% recoverable: 846,976,000 Btu/yr; displacing natural gas forced-air heat at 85% efficiency saves $5,979/yr at $0.60/therm (the footnote states $0.90/therm, inconsistent). Fan for duct loading not included. PRICE YEAR NOT STATED; 2014 gas price basis per footnote.

measure: Whole-system improvement of a neglected system
saving-unit: % of compressed-air energy (printed as 20 to 50 percent or more)
note: 100-hp example: $14,000-36,000/yr at $0.10/kWh. Audits frequently decrease energy consumption 20-50% or more (p.99). CAC: 30-60% typically achievable with affordable projects; average 17% realized by seminar participants; 15-25% cost savings from better production and use (p.106).

measure: Replace inappropriate uses (open blowing/air bars, air motors)
saving-unit: compressor hp for cabinet cooling (open tube vs refrigerated/air-to-air cooler)
note: Air motors need at least 7-8 hp of compressor power per hp of output.

measure: Variable speed drive compressor as trim machine
note: No percentage saving printed. Best efficiency between 30 and 80% speed; at full output a VSD compressor uses more power than a fixed-speed unit (drive losses); some designs unload at 40-50% speed with 10-15% unloaded power.
